assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Brain
items.clue: The organ that controls complex behaviour.

items.label: Hyperopia (long sightedness)
items.clue: A defect of the eye in which rays of light focus behind the retina.

items.label: Accommodation
items.clue: The process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects.

items.label: Iris
items.clue: The coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil, and so controls how much light enters the eye.

questions.stem: A patient can no longer coordinate their movements or keep their balance after an injury to the brain. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: Damage within the medulla
The cerebellum is damaged
Cerebral cortex is damaged
Damage to the spinal cord

questions.explanation: The cerebellum is the region of the brain responsible for coordinating muscular activity and balance, which are the functions the patient has lost.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly relates a structure of the eye to its function?

options.text: The cornea changes shape to focus images.
The iris narrows the pupil in dim lighting.
The ciliary muscles relax for near objects.
The retina contains receptors for light.

questions.explanation: The eye is a sense organ containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour, and these receptors are found in the retina at the back of the eye.

questions.stem: A person is exercising hard and their body temperature rises above normal. What happens in the skin?

options.text: Blood vessels dilate and sweat is produced.
Blood vessels move nearer the skin surface.
Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
The skin cools the body without the brain.

questions.explanation: If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced from the sweat glands; both mechanisms cause a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.

questions.stem: A person walks out of bright sunlight into a dark room. What happens in the eye?

options.text: The iris muscles make the pupil narrower.
The ciliary muscles make the lens thicker.
The cornea changes shape to admit light.
The iris muscles make the pupil wider.

questions.explanation: The eye adapts to dim light by the iris muscles widening the pupil, so more light enters the eye and reaches the receptors in the retina.

questions.stem: A student looks up from a book and focuses on a tree in the distance. What happens in the eye?

options.text: The ciliary muscles contract and the lens thickens.
The suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens bulges.
The cornea changes shape and the lens stays thin.
The ciliary muscles relax and the lens is pulled thin.

questions.explanation: To focus on a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is pulled thin, so it only slightly refracts the light rays.

questions.stem: A ray diagram shows light from a distant object coming to a focus in front of the retina. Which defect is shown, and how is it corrected?

options.text: Myopia, corrected with a convex lens.
Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens.
Myopia, corrected with a concave lens.
Hyperopia, corrected with a concave lens.

questions.explanation: Rays focusing in front of the retina show myopia (short sightedness); a concave spectacle lens spreads the rays out so that they do focus on the retina.

questions.stem: Neuroscientists want to find out which region of a patient's brain controls speech. Which statement explains why this is difficult?

options.text: Damaged brain regions are simple to repair.
MRI scanning shows which cells are working.
Each region of the brain does the same job.
The brain is complex and easily damaged.

questions.explanation: The brain is made of billions of interconnected neurones, and its complexity and delicacy make investigating brain function and treating brain damage and disease very difficult.

questions.stem: A person waits at a bus stop in cold weather and their body temperature begins to fall. How does the body raise it again?

options.text: Blood vessels dilate and shivering begins.
Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
Narrowing blood vessels cause the shivering.
The skin warms the blood without using the brain.

questions.explanation: If the body temperature is too low, blood vessels constrict (vasoconstriction) and sweating stops, reducing energy transfer from the skin, while skeletal muscles contract (shiver), releasing energy that warms the body.
